name: Wahhabism
info: Wahhabism is a Salafi revivalist movement within Sunni Islam, named after the Hanbali scholar Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, which began in Najd in the early 18th century and became bound to the Saudi ruling family.

facts.where: Najd in central Arabia, later the wider Arabian Peninsula, Mecca and Medina; Saudi Arabia and Qatar, the two countries whose native population is predominantly Wahhabi, and, through Saudi funding, mosques, schools and scholarships across the Muslim world
facts.period: began in the early 18th century; pact with Muhammad ibn Saud 1744; three Saudi States, the first ending with the destruction of Diriyah in 1818; Third Saudi State and Saudi Arabia's oil revenues from 1939; changes to Saudi religious policy from 2017
facts.figures: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab (1703–1792), the movement's founder; Muhammad ibn Saud, the local leader of the pact; Hamad ibn Nasir ibn Mu'ammar, who set out its legal theory; Abd al-Rahman ibn Hasan and Abd al-Latif ibn Abd al-Rahman, heads of the religious estate; Abd al-Aziz ibn Baz and Muhammad ibn al-Uthaymeen, leading scholars of the 20th century
facts.outcome: Ibn Abd al-Wahhab's teachings were the official creed of the three Saudi States for more than two centuries; the movement shaped Saudi Arabia's religious institutions and, with Saudi money, spread widely, while its critics call it a deviant sect and its followers reject the name

t: Followers called themselves Muwahhidun, 'the Monotheists'; the name Wahhabi was probably first used by Ibn Abd al-Wahhab's critic and brother Sulayman, and present-day followers continue to reject it, often calling themselves Salafi.
In 1744 Ibn Abd al-Wahhab formed a pact with the local leader Muhammad ibn Saud, a politico-religious alliance with the Saudi monarchy that lasted for more than 250 years.

Its central teaching holds that devotion to any being other than God, including the veneration of saints at their tombs, is shirk, while its opponents accused it of Kharijite excess and of readiness to declare other Muslims unbelievers.

sections.background:
Wahhabism arose in Najd, the central Arabian region, where rituals honouring Muslim saints and pilgrimages to their tombs and shrines were widespread. Its founder, the Hanbali scholar Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab (1703–1792), and his followers drew on the Hanbali scholar Ibn Taymiyya (1263–1328), who had advocated a return to the purity of the first three generations, the salaf, to rid Muslims of bid'a, or innovation. They regarded his works as core references in theology, although the movement also repudiated taqlid to legal authorities, Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn Qayyim among them.

The movement belonged to the revivalist trends of the 18th and 19th centuries, including the Mahdist movement in Sudan, the Senussi in Libya, the Fulani movement of Uthman Dan Fodio, the Faraizi movement in Bengal, Sayyid Ahmed Barelvi's Mujahidin and the Padri movement in Indonesia. These sought reform through a direct return to the Quran and hadith and blamed Muslim decline on the infiltration of local beliefs and practices. An earlier Ottoman movement, the Kadizadeli of the 17th century, likewise condemned practices it saw as bid'ah.

Socio-politically, the movement has been described as the first major Arab-led revolt against the Turkish, Persian and other foreign empires that had dominated the Islamic world since the Mongol invasions and the fall of the Abbasid Caliphate in the 13th century. Ibn Abd al-Wahhab's father is reported to have criticised his son when he began public preaching at Huraymila, but the sources do not state the nature of the disagreement.
sections.aims:
The first aim was tawhid, the oneness of God. All Muslims uphold it; according to David Commins and others, the disagreement between Wahhabis and their opponents is over what constitutes it. Ibn Abd al-Wahhab held that correct worship was the test of belief and that any act or statement showing devotion to a being other than God was shirk, tantamount to idolatry. He included in such acts popular practices that made holy men intercessors with God, and in his Kitab al-Tawhid he denounced the veneration of trees and rocks. He accepted that Muhammad would intercede for believers, but only by God's permission. David Commins calls it the pivotal idea that Muslims who disagreed with his definition of monotheism stood outside Islam altogether.

On takfir, Ibn Abd al-Wahhab wrote that he declared unbelievers only those who knew the religion of the Messenger and then insulted it, forbade people from it or showed enmity towards its practitioners. The movement rejected taqlid, imitation of past legal opinion, and upheld ijtihad, independent reasoning from the Quran and hadith. Its adherents also urged al-wala' wa al-bara', loyalty and disassociation, which Ibn Abd al-Wahhab argued meant Muslims should not befriend or imitate non-Muslims or heretical Muslims.

He defined armed jihad as requiring a valid religious justification and declaration by an Imam, and described the campaigns of the Emirate of Diriyah as defensive. He taught that a Muslim ruler is owed allegiance so long as he leads according to the Shari'ah, and that counsel to rulers should be private.
sections.events:
In 1744 Ibn Abd al-Wahhab formed a pact with a local leader, Muhammad bin Saud, offering political obedience and promising that protection and propagation of the movement meant 'power and glory' and rule of 'lands and men'. The state-building of the Emirate of Diriyah led to military conflicts with rival tribal chiefs; Ibn Abd al-Wahhab advised the emir on tactics, urging a largely defensive strategy and adherence to Islamic rules of warfare. After his retirement in 1773, the emir Abdulaziz, Muhammad ibn Saud's son and successor, launched offensive campaigns. Abdullah ibn Muhammad Aal Ash-Shaykh condemned military excesses during the conquest of Mecca, saying Arabs would not be taken captive and that killing women and children was not agreed to. The Emirate of Diriyah was destroyed in 1818, at the end of the Wahhabi Wars.

In 1871 the Ottomans annexed Al-Hasa, a majority-Shia area, with British help; from then Abd al-Latif ibn Abd al-Rahman wrote tracts condemning Ottomans, Shia and British as polytheists and forbade Muslims to travel or stay in their lands. Ibn Saud conquered Mecca in October 1924, and after the discovery of petroleum in 1939 oil revenues funded the spread of Wahhabi ideals. In the Hejaz, Ibn Saud imposed Wahhabi doctrines in a progressively gentler form.

Debate led Saudi authorities to allow paper money in 1951, the abolition of slavery in 1962, girls' education in 1964 and television in 1965. In 1963 the clergy expelled the scholar al-Albani after he issued a fatwa permitting women to uncover their faces.
sections.people:
Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab (1703–1792) was the founder and eponym. His son Abd Allah (1752–1826) headed the movement after his father retired in 1773 and, after the fall of the first Saudi emirate, died in exile in Cairo. His grandson Sulayman ibn Abd Allah (1780–1818) wrote an influential treatise restricting travel to and residence in the land of idolaters. His brother Sulayman ibn Abd al-Wahhab, an ardent critic, probably first used the name Wahhabi. Fatimah, his daughter, was a scholar who travelled widely and taught men and women. Muhammad ibn Saud was the local leader of the 1744 pact.

The legal jurist Hamad ibn Nasir ibn Mu'ammar (1747–1810), a son-in-law and pupil of Ibn Abd al-Wahhab, set out the movement's legal theory in a treatise on ijtihad and taqlid. Abd al-Rahman ibn Hasan led the religious estate in the second Saudi emirate, and his son Abd al-Latif ibn Abd al-Rahman (1810–1876) headed it in the 1860s and early 1870s. Ahmad al-Hifzi, a former Sufi, led the movement in Asir. Ghaliyya al-Wahhabiyya, a Bedouin woman from Turubah, rose to the rank of Amira al-Umara and led Wahhabi forces defending Mecca in the Ottoman–Wahhabi war.

In the 20th century Muhammad ibn Ibrahim Al ash-Sheikh (1893–1969), Grand Mufti from 1953, was said to have dominated the religious estate. Abd al-Aziz ibn Baz (1910–1999) has been called the most prominent proponent of the movement in his time, and Muhammad ibn al-Uthaymeen (1925–2001) another giant. Muhammad Rashid Rida, a Salafiyya reformer, worked to rehabilitate the Wahhabis in the Islamic world.
sections.outcomes:
The pact of 1744 established a politico-religious alliance with the Saudi monarchy that lasted for more than 250 years, and for more than two centuries Ibn Abd al-Wahhab's teachings were championed as the official creed in the three Saudi States. After the unification of Saudi Arabia the movement consolidated its rule over Mecca and Medina, and Saudi oil revenues spent on books, schools, universities, mosques and scholarships gave Wahhabi ideals a 'preeminent position of strength' in Islam around the world.

Estimates of Saudi spending abroad include upward of $100 billion and $2–3 billion a year since 1975; Peter Mandaville calls such figures unreliable. Khaled Abou El Fadl names four causes of the movement's reach: Arab nationalism's welcome of a revolt against the Ottomans, the call for a return to the salaf through ijtihad, control of Mecca and Medina, and the oil industry.

At home the religious establishment's position has changed. Changes to Saudi religious policy by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman since 2017 have led to crackdowns on Islamists, and by 2021 the waning power of the clerics and a nationalist narrative led to what has been described as a 'post-Wahhabi era'. Saudi Arabia's Founding Day, commemorated since 2022 on 22 February, marks Muhammad ibn Saud's ascension in 1727 and de-emphasises the 1744 pact, which has led to an official uncoupling of the clergy from the state.
sections.legacy:
The name remains contested. Followers call themselves Muwahhidun or, now, Salafi, and the name is mainly an exonym that its opponents used. King Salman has called the term a doctrine that does not exist in Saudi Arabia. Scholars differ on how it relates to Salafism: Ahmad Moussalli says all Wahhabis are Salafists but not all Salafists are Wahhabis. The Syrian-Albanian scholar al-Albani called Ibn Abd al-Wahhab a Salafi in creed but not in fiqh, and the Saudi clergy expelled him in 1963.

Critics among other Muslims have called the movement a deviant sect. The Ottoman Hanafi scholar Ibn Abidin declared it a modern manifestation of the Kharijites, and Sunni clerics of Al-Azhar called it a satanic faith. Supporters include Muhammad Iqbal, who called it the first throb of life in modern Islam while noting that its vision of the past was uncritical, and Taha Hussein, who credited it with awakening the Arab soul.

On militancy, the claims are disputed. A study commissioned by the European Parliament in 2013, by Claude Moniquet, named Wahhabism the main source of global terrorism; others hold that al-Qaeda and Islamic State are not Wahhabi, and that Saudi senior scholars condemned suicide bombing. Scholars also note that post-Soviet governments and others use the label for any Islamic assertion or opposition.

summary: Wahhabism is a Salafi revivalist movement in Sunni Islam that began in Najd in the early 18th century around Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab and, from the pact of 1744, was bound to the Saudi family. Its followers reject the name; its critics call it a deviant sect, and its influence spread widely with Saudi funding.
references: David Commins, The Wahhabi Mission and Saudi Arabia (I. B. Tauris, 2006)
Natana J. DeLong-Bas, Wahhabi Islam: From Revival and Reform to Global Jihad (Oxford University Press, 2004)
Simon Ross Valentine, Force and Fanaticism: Wahhabism in Saudi Arabia and Beyond (C. Hurst & Co., 2015)
